title: Week 117 · Lesson 141: Cognitive Change, Dementia, Delirium & Capacity — FNP-Level Diagnostic and Safety Care
html:
PHASE 5 · FAMILY & LIFESPAN PRIMARY CARE

Week 117 — Lesson 141: Cognitive Change, Dementia, Delirium & Capacity

FNP-level goal: Evaluate cognitive and behavioral change through time course, attention, cognitive domains, function, collateral history, medications, mood, sensory status, laboratory and imaging context; distinguish delirium from chronic neurocognitive disease; communicate diagnosis honestly; and protect autonomy, safety, and caregiver capacity.

Learning Objectives

  • Differentiate normal aging, subjective cognitive concern, mild cognitive impairment, dementia, depression, and delirium.
  • Use validated cognitive and informant tools as part of—not substitutes for—a diagnostic evaluation.
  • Recognize clinical patterns that suggest Alzheimer, vascular, Lewy body, frontotemporal, or other causes.
  • Identify medication, metabolic, sensory, sleep, psychiatric, neurologic, and social contributors.
  • Assess decision-specific capacity, driving, medication, financial, wandering, firearm, and caregiver safety.

Part 1 — Take the Concern Seriously

Memory complaints may be reported by the patient, family, staff, or clinician observation. Ask what changed, when it began, whether the change is progressive or stepwise, and which daily activities are affected. A patient may minimize deficits because of fear or reduced insight; a family may overinterpret normal lapses. Both perspectives need respectful assessment.

NIA emphasizes that early assessment can identify reversible contributors, clarify diagnosis, address safety, support planning, and connect caregivers with resources. Do not dismiss concern because the patient is socially fluent during a short visit.

Part 2 — Cognition Includes More Than Memory

Assess learning and recall, attention, executive function, language, visuospatial ability, social cognition, and behavior. Ask for real-world examples: repeated bills, missed medicines, getting lost, unsafe cooking, word-finding, poor judgment, personality change, or difficulty using familiar tools.

Document baseline education, occupation, language, literacy, hearing, vision, cultural context, and prior neurologic or psychiatric history. Test performance must be interpreted within these factors.

Part 3 — Function Defines Clinical Impact

Mild cognitive impairment involves objective cognitive change with relative preservation of independent everyday function. Dementia, also termed major neurocognitive disorder in diagnostic frameworks, interferes with independent function. The boundary depends on what the person can do safely and accurately, not one score.

Review medication, finances, driving, shopping, cooking, communication, appointment management, and basic ADLs. Compensatory strategies may conceal decline: a spouse may have silently taken over bills or medication months earlier.

Part 4 — Establish the Time Course Before the Score

Hours to days with fluctuation and inattention suggests delirium. Weeks may reflect medication, depression, infection, metabolic disease, subacute neurologic disease, or rapidly progressive dementia. Months to years suggests neurodegenerative or vascular disease, though mixed pathology is common.

Sudden focal deficit, severe headache, seizure, head injury, rapid loss of consciousness, or abrupt cognitive change requires emergency neurologic evaluation rather than routine memory testing.

Part 5 — Delirium: Acute and Fluctuating

Delirium is an acute disturbance in attention and awareness caused by an underlying medical, toxic, withdrawal, or environmental stressor. It can be hyperactive, hypoactive, or mixed. Hypoactive delirium appears as sleepiness, reduced interaction, slow movement, or poor intake and is easily mistaken for depression or advanced dementia.

Look for infection, hypoxia, hypoglycemia, electrolyte disturbance, dehydration, pain, constipation, urinary retention, organ failure, medication toxicity, anticholinergic burden, sedative or alcohol withdrawal, stroke, seizure, trauma, and sleep disruption. Dementia is a major risk factor but does not explain an acute change.

Part 6 — Delirium Management

Treat the cause and stabilize physiology. Reorient, mobilize, restore glasses and hearing aids, support sleep-wake rhythm, hydrate, manage pain, avoid unnecessary devices, and involve familiar caregivers. Review every new and recently stopped medicine.

Antipsychotics do not treat delirium itself and can cause sedation, falls, stroke, cardiac effects, and death. They may be considered only for severe distress or immediate danger after reversible causes and nonpharmacologic measures are addressed, using the lowest-risk individualized plan and frequent reassessment.

Part 7 — Cognitive Screening Is Not Diagnosis

Select a validated brief tool suited to language, culture, sensory ability, education, and setting. Ensure hearing aids and glasses are available and avoid testing during acute illness when possible. Include an informant-based measure when insight or test conditions are uncertain.

A low score may reflect delirium, depression, limited education, language mismatch, sleep, medication, or neurologic disease. A normal score does not erase compelling functional decline. Positive findings lead to a full evaluation; they do not independently identify etiology.

Part 8 — Focused Diagnostic Evaluation

Review medical, neurologic, psychiatric, sleep, substance, family, trauma, and medication history. Perform physical and neurologic examination, gait, sensory assessment, mood evaluation, and functional review. Common laboratory evaluation is individualized but often addresses blood count, metabolic and organ function, thyroid, vitamin B12, glucose, and other risk-based causes.

Structural brain imaging may be indicated to assess vascular disease, mass, hydrocephalus, subdural collection, or other pathology, especially with focal findings, unusual course, younger onset, rapid progression, gait or urinary pattern, or head trauma. Biomarkers and advanced imaging are used selectively, often with specialty guidance.

Part 9 — Alzheimer Pattern

Typical Alzheimer disease often begins insidiously with progressive difficulty learning and retaining new information, followed by impairment in other domains. Functional decline advances over time. Atypical language, visuospatial, or executive presentations occur.

Do not diagnose solely from age plus forgetfulness. Establish objective decline, functional impact, course, and exclusion or contribution of delirium, medication, depression, sleep disorder, vascular disease, and other neurologic conditions.

Part 10 — Vascular Cognitive Impairment

Vascular disease may produce slowed processing, impaired executive function, gait change, focal neurologic signs, or stepwise decline, although presentations vary. Neurodegenerative and vascular pathology frequently coexist. Review stroke history, atrial fibrillation, blood pressure, diabetes, lipids, tobacco, sleep apnea, and activity.

Preventing further vascular injury is central, but targets should be individualized to avoid orthostasis, hypoglycemia, or medication burden that worsens function.

Part 11 — Lewy Body Pattern

Dementia with Lewy bodies may include fluctuating cognition, recurrent well-formed visual hallucinations, REM sleep behavior disorder, parkinsonism, and autonomic dysfunction. Medication sensitivity is important; dopamine-blocking antipsychotics can cause severe worsening, particularly with classic agents.

Differentiate visual hallucinations in chronic disease from acute delirium and medication effects. Specialty collaboration is often appropriate.

Part 12 — Frontotemporal Pattern

Frontotemporal disorders may present earlier than typical Alzheimer disease with disinhibition, apathy, loss of empathy, compulsive behavior, dietary change, impaired judgment, or progressive language disorder while memory initially appears less affected. Psychiatric misdiagnosis is common.

New personality or language change with functional decline requires neurologic evaluation, especially at younger ages or with relevant family history.

Part 13 — Depression and Cognitive Symptoms

Depression can impair attention, processing speed, motivation, sleep, and memory. Ask about mood, anhedonia, guilt, energy, appetite, psychomotor change, hopelessness, and suicide risk. Depression and neurocognitive disease can coexist; improvement in mood does not always normalize cognition.

Use validated mood tools but do not force a false choice between “depression” and “dementia” before longitudinal reassessment.

Part 14 — Medication and Substance Effects

Review anticholinergics, sedatives, benzodiazepines, opioids, sleep products, antihistamines, muscle relaxants, bladder medicines, corticosteroids, antiseizure agents, and polypharmacy. Ask alcohol, cannabis, and other substances plus adherence, duplication, withdrawal, and kidney or liver change.

Deprescribe carefully with indication review and tapering when needed. Avoid replacing one sedative with another without addressing sleep, pain, anxiety, or environment.

Part 15 — Sleep, Hearing, Vision, and Pain

Untreated hearing or vision loss can look like confusion and worsen isolation. Sleep apnea, insomnia, REM sleep behavior disorder, restless legs, and circadian disruption affect cognition and may provide diagnostic clues. Persistent pain consumes attention, while sedating pain treatment may worsen it.

Restore sensory aids and treat sleep and pain as part of the cognitive plan, not as unrelated problems.

Part 16 — Communicating the Diagnosis

Ask how much detail the patient wants and whom they want involved. Explain findings in plain language, distinguish certainty from uncertainty, and allow time for emotion and questions. Avoid vague reassurance when impairment is present, but do not declare a specific disease without adequate evidence.

Provide a written plan: additional testing, follow-up, medication changes, safety actions, support resources, and who owns each step. A diagnosis without ongoing care coordination can increase fear without improving safety.

Part 17 — Treatment and Risk Reduction

Management includes physical activity, vascular risk optimization, hearing and vision care, sleep treatment, social and cognitive engagement, nutrition, medication reduction, and caregiver support. Symptomatic medicines such as cholinesterase inhibitors or memantine are selected by diagnosis, stage, contraindication, adverse effects, and goals; they are not universal memory enhancers.

Newer disease-modifying anti-amyloid treatments require confirmation of appropriate Alzheimer biology, staging, genetic and bleeding-risk considerations, MRI monitoring for amyloid-related imaging abnormalities, infusion infrastructure, and specialty shared decision-making. They are not routine empiric primary-care prescriptions for any memory complaint.

Part 18 — Behavioral and Psychological Symptoms

When agitation, resistance, wandering, hallucination, or sleep reversal occurs, first define the behavior and trigger. Look for pain, fear, constipation, retention, infection, hunger, overstimulation, loneliness, caregiver approach, and environment. Modify causes and communication before sedating.

Immediate danger may require emergency evaluation. Medication decisions require explicit target symptom, risk-benefit discussion, time-limited trial, monitoring, and deprescribing plan.

Part 19 — Capacity Is Decision Specific

Capacity asks whether the patient can understand relevant information, appreciate how it applies, reason about choices, and communicate a decision. It is not determined by age, diagnosis, cognitive score, family disagreement, or an unconventional choice alone.

Enhance capacity by treating delirium, reducing pain, using hearing and visual aids, simplifying information, and choosing the best time of day. If capacity is lacking, identify the legally authorized surrogate while preserving the patient's participation and preferences.

Part 20 — Safety Domains

Assess medication errors, unpaid bills, scams, unsafe cooking, wandering, falls, firearms, driving, living alone, exploitation, and emergency response. Driving risk clues include crashes, near misses, getting lost, traffic violations, family concern, visuospatial impairment, slowed reaction, and sedating medication. Follow state law and use formal driving evaluation when needed.

Firearms and other lethal means should be discussed respectfully when cognitive, mood, impulsivity, or household safety concerns exist. Create specific rather than generic plans.

Part 21 — Caregiver Health and Systems

Ask the caregiver about workload, sleep, health, depression, finances, confidence, conflict, and respite. Validate strain without assuming the patient must leave home. Connect families to social work, home services, adult day programs, respite, legal and financial planning, and disease-specific education.

Missed medication, malnutrition, or poor hygiene may reflect insufficient resources rather than intentional neglect, but immediate safety must still be protected.

Part 22 — When to Refer

Refer for younger onset, rapid progression, atypical presentation, focal findings, movement disorder, seizures, complex psychiatric symptoms, diagnostic uncertainty, need for neuropsychological testing, advanced biomarker evaluation, or disease-modifying therapy consideration. Emergency evaluation is required for acute delirium with instability, stroke signs, seizure, head injury, severe medication toxicity, inability to maintain hydration, or immediate danger.

Clinical Case 1 — The Quiet Delirium

An 84-year-old with stable dementia becomes drowsy, inattentive, and stops eating two days after starting an anticholinergic bladder drug. The FNP recognizes hypoactive delirium, stops assuming progression, and arranges urgent medication and medical-cause evaluation.

Clinical Case 2 — Normal Brief Screen, Unsafe Function

A retired accountant scores within the expected range on a brief test but has repeated financial fraud, unpaid bills, and getting lost. The FNP values collateral functional evidence, completes a broader evaluation, and addresses financial and driving safety rather than dismissing concern.

Clinical Case 3 — Hallucinations and Medication Sensitivity

A 75-year-old has fluctuating cognition, visual hallucinations, dream enactment, and parkinsonism. The FNP considers Lewy body disease, avoids reflex dopamine-blocking treatment, reviews delirium and medications, and coordinates specialty assessment.

FNP High-Yield Framework: COGNITION

  1. C — Course first: hours, weeks, months, progressive, stepwise, fluctuating.
  2. O — Obtain collateral and function: IADLs, ADLs, errors, change from baseline.
  3. G — Gauge domains: attention, memory, executive, language, visuospatial, behavior.
  4. N — Name reversible contributors: delirium, drugs, depression, sleep, senses, metabolic disease.
  5. I — Investigate the pattern: examination, labs, imaging, disease phenotype, referral.
  6. T — Treat causes and support reserve: vascular, activity, hearing, sleep, medication, caregiver.
  7. I — Individualize capacity and treatment: specific decision, goals, benefit, burden.
  8. O — Organize safety: driving, medicines, money, cooking, wandering, firearms.
  9. N — Navigate follow-up: disclosure, result owner, advance planning, crisis signs.

Take-Home Summary

Cognitive care starts with time course and function. A brief score does not diagnose dementia, a dementia diagnosis does not explain acute decline, and cognitive impairment does not automatically eliminate capacity. FNP-level care connects etiologic evaluation with medication review, safety, honest communication, and caregiver support.

Educational note: Follow current NIA, Alzheimer’s Association DETeCD-ADRD, AGS delirium, local capacity, driving, and emergency guidance. Acute inattention, focal neurologic change, seizure, head injury, severe toxicity, inability to maintain essential care, or immediate danger requires urgent evaluation.
